content:
You can learn a great deal about an area before buying a demographic report. The harder part is keeping track of which place, population and time period each number describes.

This guide walks you through U.S. Census Bureau data, USPS delivery routes and local planning resources. You will finish with a short area brief that another leader can check and update.

---

## 1. Name the area you are studying

Write down the question first. Are you describing a city, comparing nearby areas or checking the streets around a possible meeting location? Record the state, county and exact place name before searching.

Start with a named Census geography, such as a city or census tract. If you use several tracts, list each one and retain a map. Label this as your chosen study area. Do not present it as an official neighborhood boundary unless you have checked that boundary with the local agency.

Census ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, called ZCTAs, approximate the distribution of postal ZIP Codes. They are not delivery routes, and some valid postal ZIP Codes have no corresponding ZCTA. Keep those labels separate in your notes.

---

## 2. Choose the right Census product

The American Community Survey, or ACS, describes social, economic, housing and demographic characteristics. Its figures are survey estimates. For population totals, the Census Bureau recommends the decennial census or its Population Estimates Program instead.

| Your question | Starting point |
|---|---|
| What are the area's characteristics? | ACS data profiles |
| What does a small area look like? | ACS five-year estimates |
| What is the population total? | Decennial census or Population Estimates Program |

Standard ACS one-year estimates cover areas with at least 65,000 people. Five-year estimates cover smaller areas, including census tracts. A five-year estimate combines observations across that period. Its ending year does not make it a snapshot of that single year.

<Callout type="important">
Tool instructions and availability were checked October 15, 2026. Before using a figure, confirm the current release, geography and period with the U.S. Census Bureau. Confirm current routes and any mailing requirements with USPS before planning a mailing.
</Callout>

---

## 3. Retrieve the ACS profiles

Open data.census.gov. Search for your place and a table ID, or use its filters to select the geography and survey product. Filters are useful for tracts with complex names. Check the selected geography again whenever you change tables.

The Census Bureau identifies these profile tables:

| Table ID | Profile subject |
|---|---|
| DP02 | Social characteristics |
| DP03 | Economic characteristics |
| DP04 | Housing characteristics |
| DP05 | Demographic and housing estimates |

- [ ] Select your geography and the ACS one-year or five-year product.
- [ ] Choose the period and open the profile you need.
- [ ] Read the row labels, population covered and table notes before copying figures.
- [ ] Keep margins of error visible.
- [ ] Download the table and save its source information.

The Download control offers Excel, CSV and ZIP formats. Excel includes an Information worksheet with source details, the population covered and table notes. CSV has less explanatory information, so save those details separately if you choose CSV. A download can preserve hidden columns or removed margins of error. Check the file you saved.

---

## 4. Check uncertainty before comparing

The Census Bureau publishes a margin of error for every ACS estimate to help you assess reliability. Read it alongside the estimate. If uncertainty is large relative to the figure, mark the result as uncertain before using it in a planning discussion.

For comparisons, use the same product and check that the geography and definition still match. Compare one-year estimates with one-year estimates, or five-year estimates with five-year estimates. Follow Census guidance to compare non-overlapping five-year periods. Adjacent releases share observations and should not be treated as independent annual measurements.

<Callout type="warning">
A difference between two displayed estimates does not by itself establish a real change. Check margins of error and the Census Bureau's comparison guidance before describing an area as growing, shrinking or changing.
</Callout>

If a comparison matters to a major decision, ask a Census data specialist or local planning analyst to help interpret it. Keep their explanation with the tables.

---

## 5. Look at USPS delivery routes

USPS provides the Every Door Direct Mail Online Tool, often called EDDM. Search by address, city and state, or ZIP Code. Use Show Table to inspect neighborhood routes. The tool includes demographic filters such as age, household size and income.

Record the route identifiers and the date you looked them up. Keep any route counts under their displayed labels. Do not relabel delivery addresses as people, or substitute a route total for an ACS population estimate.

Use this step to understand postal coverage. Stop before ordering or paying if you are only researching. Mailing design, postage and campaign decisions require their own current checks.

---

## 6. Ask local planning for context

Search your city or county's official website for its planning department, population reports and open-data resources. Ask which published geography best matches the area you mean.

For a concrete example, New York City's Department of City Planning maintains Population FactFinder. Its documentation describes selecting study areas to produce population profiles. That is an example of a local resource, not a tool covering every city.

Ask your local office these questions:

- Which report or map should I use for this area?
- What period does it describe, and when was it updated?
- Is a figure an observed count, a survey estimate or a projection?
- Have boundaries or definitions changed since the earlier report?

Save the report title and the answer you receive. Do not assume a local dashboard uses newer data just because its page looks recent.

---

## 7. Keep the limits in the brief

The Census Bureau's faith-community guidance explains that the decennial census does not collect religious affiliation. Do not use these profiles to count church attenders or label households as believers or nonbelievers.

Also avoid assigning an area's average characteristics to an individual resident. If a report describes a tract, label your finding as a tract finding. Keep conclusions about a person's circumstances out of the spreadsheet.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him."* — Proverbs 18:13 (LSB)
</Callout>

Keep questions raised by the data in a separate part of your notes. A question to investigate is different from a finding supported by a table.

---

## 8. Save a brief someone else can check

Attach your map and original downloads. For every figure you keep, record the publisher, table ID, row label, geography, period, estimate, margin of error if supplied, source location and access date.

<Callout type="tip">
Start your brief with the area definition and data period. A reader should be able to tell what the figures describe before reaching the first number.
</Callout>

- [ ] Keep Census areas and postal routes clearly labeled.
- [ ] Separate source findings from questions and local observations.
- [ ] Flag missing information and uncertain comparisons.
- [ ] Record who will check the sources again before the brief informs a decision.

Share the brief and its files together. Another leader should be able to locate the same tables, understand the limits and correct a figure without repeating your whole search.
excerpt: Find Census profiles, inspect USPS routes and check local planning sources. Save an area brief with clear boundaries, dates and limits.
title: Finding Demographic Data for Your Area
